hooks.text: Think the Moon doesn't spin? That is a total myth.
The Moon spins on its axis every single lunar orbit.
Why can we only see one side of our own Moon?

title: The Myth of the Moon's Dark Side
description: Discover how tidal locking synchronizes the Moon's rotation and why we didn't see the far side until 1959.

beats.text: Think the Moon doesn't spin? That is a total myth.
beats.visual: Earth and Moon from space, Apollo 8 photograph, 1968
queries: Earth and Moon from space Apollo 8

beats.text: Our Moon actually rotates on its axis at the exact same speed it orbits Earth.
beats.visual: Synchronous rotation diagram showing Moon's rotation and orbit

beats.text: This synchronous tidal locking is caused by Earth's gravity stretching the lunar body into physical bulges.
beats.visual: Tidal bulge diagram illustrating Earth's gravitational pull

beats.text: Gravity pulls on these bulges like a brake, forcing the spin to match the orbit.
beats.visual: Illustration of gravitational torque acting on lunar bulges

beats.text: This constant friction slows the rotation and pushes the Moon away by four centimeters every year.
beats.visual: Illustration of the Moon drifting away from Earth

beats.text: We finally saw the far side when the Soviet Luna 3 photographed it in 1959.
beats.visual: Luna 3 spacecraft model and the first far side photographs, 1959
queries: Luna 3 far side of the Moon

beats.text: Even Pluto and its moon Charon are mutually caught in this same gravitational grip.
beats.visual: Pluto and Charon as seen by New Horizons, 2015

beats.text: This synchronization hides the far side forever, which is why people still believe the Moon doesn't spin.
beats.visual: First photograph of the far side of the Moon by Luna 3, 1959
